messages.author: 938d2cd6a714081f
messages.subject: Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model
parts:
Dear All.

Currently I am trying to specify the following hierarchical 3PL Item Response model in Stan. It is an extension of the hierarchical 2PL model illustrated by Furr (in the Stan-Tutorials). The model itself is specified according to Glas & van der Linden (2003). Alpha (item discrimination), beta (item difficulties), and gamma (the pseudo-guessing parameter) are correlated draws from a multinormal distribution and are summarized in a vector ksi in the following way: xi = {log(a), b, logit(c)}. 

I specified the model in Stan as follows:

model_3hpl <- '
data {
    int<lower=1> I;                 // # items
    int<lower=1> J;                 // # persons
    int<lower=1> N;                 // # observations
    int<lower=1, upper=I> ii[N];
    int<lower=1, upper=J> jj[N];
    int<lower=0, upper=1> y[N];
}

parameters {
    vector[J] theta;          // # abilities
    vector[3] xi[I];          // # alpha/beta/gamma vector
    vector[3] mu;             // # alpha/beta/gamma means
    vector<lower=0>[3] tau;   // # alpha/beta/gamma res.sds
    cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Omega;  // # correlation matrix
}

transformed parameters {
     vector[I] alpha;
     vector[I] beta;
     vector[I] gamma;
      for (i in 1:I) {          // # deriving alpha/beta/gamma from xi
       alpha[i] <- exp(xi[i, 1]);
       beta[i] <- xi[i, 2];
       gamma[i] <- inv_logit(xi[i, 3]);
      }
}

model {
    xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));
    L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);

    theta ~ normal(0,1);

    mu[1] ~ normal(0,1);
    mu[2] ~ normal(0,5);
    mu[3] ~ normal(-1,1);

    tau ~ exponential(.1);

     for (n in 1:N)
        y[n] ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii[n]]+(1-gamma[ii[n]])*inv_logit(alpha[ii[n]]*(theta[jj[n]]-beta[ii[n]])));
}

generated quantities {
    corr_matrix[3] Omega;
    Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);
}'

The model runs, convergence is fairly well. However, I'm afraid there are some misspecifications, because parameter recovery for mu[3] and tau[3] are not that good. The prior on mu[3] is specified as normal(-1,1), since the pseudo-guessing parameter c is on the logit scale and thus is upward bound at zero. 

Are there any misspecifications, or do I miss something obvious?

If somebody wants to replicate my results, here is the code for the data simulation, adapted from Furr(2016).

# Set paramters for the simulated data
I <- 10
J <- 500
mu <- c(0, 0, -1.38)
tau <- c(0.25, 1, 0.75)
Omega <- matrix(c(1, 0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 1, -0.3, 0.1, 0.3, 1), ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE) #negative corr c & difficulty b

# Calculate or sample remaining paramters
set.seed(25)
Sigma <- tau %*% t(tau) * Omega
xi <- MASS::mvrnorm(I, c(0, 0, -1.38), Sigma)
alpha <- exp(mu[1] + as.vector(xi[, 1]))
beta <- as.vector(mu[2] + xi[, 2])
gamma <- inv.logit(as.vector(xi[, 3]))
theta <- rnorm(J, mean = 0, sd = 1)

# Assemble data and simulate response
data_list <- list(I = I, J = J, N = I * J, ii = rep(1:I, times = J), jj = rep(1:J, each = I))
delta <- alpha[data_list$ii] * (theta[data_list$jj] - beta[data_list$ii])
eta <- gamma[data_list$ii] + (1 - gamma[data_list$ii]) * inv.logit(delta)
data_list$y <- as.numeric(eta > runif(data_list$N))
propCorr <- (sum(data_list$y))/(data_list$N)

Any help appreciated! Thank you!

Best, 
Chris

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model
parts:
I'd suggest just keeping everything on the logit scale
and directly parameterizing alpha with a <lower=0> constraint
and gamma with a <lower=0, upper=1> constraint.

The 3PL model involves many degrees of freedom. For instance,
a problem that all students answer correctly can be explained
by it being a very easy example or one that is easy to guess.
So I wouldn't expect the relevant parameters to be well defined.

Do the posterior intervals have the right coverage? If so, there's
probably nothing wrong with the model.

The logit scale doesn't upper-bound anything at 0, but I don't
think that's relevant here. Your transforms look OK.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model

real yhat[n];
...
for(n in 1:N)
 yhat[n] = gamma[ii[n]]+(1-gamma[ii[n]])*inv_logit(alpha[ii[n]]*(theta[jj[n]]-beta[ii[n]]));

y~bernouilli(yhat);


This snippet is giving you a vectorized version of  your code. If I remember correctly, loop are not necessarily a problem but the additions to the target distribution (with ~) are better kept outside of the loops because of the autodiff behind the scenes.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model
parts:
Stijn's right---the loops are fast in Stan, and setting yhat
and then calling y ~ bernoulli(yhat) will be faster, though
it's not going to be that much faster because there aren't
any shared computations to exploit in this case---it just
eliminates some virtual function calls in the derivative
calculations.

When we get inv_logit vectorized (hopefully in the next release),
this will be a one-liner:

y ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii] + (1 - gamma[ii]) * inv_logit(alpha[ii] .* (theta[jj] - beta[ii]));

assuming all of gamma, alpha, theta, and beta are declared as vector
types (not real arrays).

- Bob

messages.author: 938d2cd6a714081f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model
parts:
Dear All,

in order to optimize the model (i.e. increase its efficiency) I tried to implement the multivariate non-centered parameterization of the model. Following the examples in the manual and various suggestions in the mailing list the code looks as follows (only the changes are illustrated, the rest of the code is equivalent to the code above):

"
parameters {
  vector[J] theta;        //abilities
  matrix[3,I] xi_tilde;   //parameter matrix
  [...]
}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,3] xi;
  xi = (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';
  [...]
}

model {
  //xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));//
  to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
  [...]
}
"

While model results are equivalent to those of the cholesky-model, the non-centered parameterization substantially increases the effective sample size of all parameters and helps with convergence. Moreover, it eliminates practically all divergent transitions (which was only possible in the cholesky-model by tuning the sampler. Hence, I hope I managed to implement the non-centered parameterzation correctly.

What I am unsure of, however, is the following statement in the model block:

to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);

 What does this statement imply exactly? The manual gives various examples for other cases, but I cannot quite get my head around my code. More specifically, I am unsure where the parameter means (vector[3] mu;) and their priors come into play?

Any help, comments, feedback appreciated!

Best, 
Chris

>

> to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
>
> What does this statement imply exactly?

It increments the log density with an independent normal prior on
each entry of the xi_tilde matrix. So basically, it's the unit
normal basis that provides z scores, which then get transformed by
rotating (correlation) and scaling (scale/variance).

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical 3PL Item Response Model
parts:
Dear Bob, Ben and Michael,

first of all I wish you all a happy new year!

Sorry to bother you again, but I have some further questions regarding the non-centered parameterization for the hierarchical 3PL model mentioned above. Following advice here on the mailing list and the examples in the user manual I was able to implement the parameterization for this model. However, I am still unsure about the role of the mus (which are the grand means of the discrimination, difficulty and pseudo-guessing parameters in this case).

I have two versions of the model:

model_A = "
[...]

parameters {
vector[J] theta;
matrix[3,I] xi_tilde;
vector[3] mu;                                          //grand means of the item parameters
vector<lower=0>[3] tau;
cholesky_factor_corr[3] L_Omega;

}

transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,3] xi;

vector[I] alpha;
  vector[I] beta;
  vector[I] gamma;
xi = (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';   //non-centering xi, but without mu
for (i in 1:I) {

alpha[I] = exp(xi[,1]);
    beta[I]  = xi[i,2];
    gamma[I] = inv_logit(xi[,3]);
  }
}

model {
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
   
  to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
  //implies: xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega)); but mu isn't specified above?
 
  theta ~ normal(0,1);

  mu[1] ~ normal(0,0.25);
  mu[2] ~ normal(0,2);
  mu[3] ~ normal(-1.3,0.25);

  tau ~ cauchy(0,1);

  y ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii] + (1-gamma[ii]) .* inv_logit(alpha[ii] .* (theta[jj] - beta[ii])));
}

[...]
"

Where are the mu's coming into play in this case? In a similar application here on the user list, Henrik Singmann mentioned that he removed the additive parameter (mu) before the parentheses, because the parameters in question were zero-centered. However, in this case only mu[1] and mu[2] are zero-centered, while mu[3] isn't.

I concluded that in order to specify the non-centering correctly, I need a matrix of grand means. Hence, the second specification of the model:

model_B = "
[...]

parameters {
[...]
matrix[I,3] mu;                                             //matrix of grand means of the item parameters
[...]
}

transformed parameters {
[...]
  xi = mu + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';   //non-centering xi, this time with mu
[...]
  }
}

model {
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
   
  to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
  //implies: xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));
 
  theta ~ normal(0,1);

  to_vector(mu[,1]) ~ normal(0,0.25);
  to_vector(mu[,2]) ~ normal(0,2);
  to_vector(mu[,3]) ~ normal(-1.3,0.25);

  tau ~ cauchy(0,1);

  y ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii] + (1-gamma[ii]) .* inv_logit(alpha[ii] .* (theta[jj] - beta[ii])));
}

[...]
"

Which one of the two models is correct? Or am I getting something completely wrong, and none of the models is correct? I am currently working on a simulation study investigating the impact of the prior for the top-level scale parameter on parameter accuracy and precision in the H3PL model, and it seems that the non-centered parameterization helps substantially with effective sample size and divergent transitions.

Thanks again for your help!

Best wishes,
Christoph

parts:
Dear Bob,

thanks for your response, sorry for my late reply. You were right, in the first version of the model the mus weren't connected to anything in the model.
I understand now that the mus are the mean locations (the overall means) for the discrimination, difficulty and pseudo-guessing parameters (alpha, beta and gamma), and
that they need to be added to xi to obtain the correct distribution(s).

I have one last question: where would I add the mus? As you mentioned, usually I'd add them to xi.
Correct me if I am wrong, but are there two alternatives to add mu to xi?

In the first, mu is a Ix3 matrix which is added to (diag_pre_multiply(tau,Omega) * xi_tilde)'.

"
[...]
transformed parameters {
[...]
  xi = mu + (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_

Omega) * xi_tilde)';  
[...]
  }
[...]
"

However, it seems odd to me that I have to estimate the three different overall means for each item (in this case 25 times for each overall mean).

"
model {
  L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
   
  to_vector(xi_tilde) ~ normal(0,1);
  //implies: xi ~ multi_normal_cholesky(mu, diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega));
 
  theta ~ normal(0,1);

  to_vector(mu[,1]) ~ normal(0,0.25);
  to_vector(mu[,2]) ~ normal(0,2);
  to_vector(mu[,3]) ~ normal(-1.3,0.25);

  tau ~ cauchy(0,1);

  y ~ bernoulli(gamma[ii] + (1-gamma[ii]) .* inv_logit(alpha[ii] .* (theta[jj] - beta[ii])));
}

[...]
"
In the second alternative, mu is a vector[3] and I add each mu to the respective column of xi in the transformed parameters block:

"
transformed parameters {
  matrix[I,3] xi;

vector<lower=0>[I] alpha;
  vector[I] beta;
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[I] gamma;
xi = (diag_pre_multiply(tau,L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';
for (i in 1:I) {

alpha[I] = exp(mu[1] + xi[,1]);
    beta[I]  = mu[2] + xi[i,2];
    gamma[I] = inv_logit(mu[3] + xi[,3]);
  }
}"

Consequently, I only need to estimate each mu once:

"
model {
[...]

mu[1] ~ normal(0,0.25);
  mu[2] ~ normal(0,2);
  mu[3] ~ normal(-1.3,0.25);

[...]
}
"

Although the estimates are reasonable in both cases, a significant advantage in terms of effective sample size is only recognizable when mu is a matrix[I,3].

I just want to make sure that I implement the non-centered parameterization correctly!

Thank you very much again!

Best wishes,
Christoph

nevermind, I got it. It's version 2 of my previous post. Results are equivalent to those of the centered model.

Moreover, divergent transitions are completely gone.

"
[...]

  vector<lower=0>[I] alpha;
  vector[I] beta;
  vector<lower=0,upper=1>[I] gamma;
xi = (diag_pre_multiply(tau, L_Omega) * xi_tilde)';
for (i in 1:I) {

alpha[i] = exp(mu[1] + xi[i,1]);
    beta[i] = mu[2] + xi[i,2];
    gamma[i] = inv_logit(mu[3] + xi[i,3]);
  }
}
[...]
"



Best wishes,
Christoph
